title: A child's hair
hookLine: combing a child's kesh, tying a small topknot and a patka
tomorrow: how do you teach a letter to a kid who can't read it yet?

cards: Saturday morning, a cartoon on, a bottle of detangling spray, and a seven-year-old who has decided this is the worst day of his life.
The whole family is busy with the new baby, so Simran is on hair duty for her little cousin Fateh. His hair has never been cut, and it reaches past his shoulders.
Halfway through the first knot he shouts it: my friend Leo's hair is short and nobody combs it. Why can't I just cut mine? Simran stops, comb in the air.
Two answers come to her at once.

teach.h: KEEP IT FROM BIRTH: WHO HE IS.
teach.b: Both answers live inside Sikh families, so let each one speak. The first: keep it from birth. Kesh, uncut hair, is one of the five Ks, and the Sikh code of conduct asks parents to keep their children's hair uncut.
Families who hold this say kesh isn't a decision a child makes at sixteen; it's simply who he is, the way he was made, from the first day.
A small boy wears his hair in a joora, a topknot, often covered with a patka, a square of cloth tied over it, until he's ready for a full turban.

teach.h: LET HIM CHOOSE: HIS OWN YES.
teach.b: The second: let him choose. Some Sikh families wait. Their best case is that a gift means most when it's chosen; they hope kesh will be his own yes, not a rule he resents.
The code takes the first side, and Simran's family has too.
But here's what both agree on, and it's the part that answers Fateh tonight. Nobody in either family wants hair to mean pain.
The kanga, the small wooden comb a Sikh keeps in the hair, is about care, not war.
Start from the ends. Hold the hair above the knot so it doesn't pull. Then the joora, and the patka tied neat on top.

how: In Sikh homes that follow the code, a child's hair is kept uncut from birth, combed with a kanga, tied in a joora and covered with a patka until the child moves to a full turban; some families wait for the child to choose.

o: the small wooden comb kept in uncut hair
a long scarf worn at weddings and feasts
a square of cloth tied over a child's topknot

games.q: Fateh's hair, piece by piece — tap the pairs.

s: kesh only matters once a Sikh takes amrit, so a child's hair doesn't count
the code asks parents to keep children's hair uncut from birth; families who hold this say it's who the child is.
some Sikh families wait and let a child choose about kesh
their best case: a gift means most when it's chosen. the code itself takes the other side.
the families who keep kesh from birth and the ones who wait disagree on everything about hair
they agree on one thing: hair should never mean pain. the kanga is about care.

games.q: your family kept your kesh from birth. your cousin's family is letting their son choose later. what's their best case?
o: a gift means most when it's chosen; they hope kesh will be his own yes.
the code tells parents to wait until a child is old enough to decide.
hair only counts after amrit, so there's nothing to decide before then.
games.why: that's the strongest version of the other side. the code itself asks parents to keep children's hair uncut, and both sides agree hair should never mean pain.

practice: Take a comb or a brush to your own hair, or simply run your fingers through it. Go slowly, starting from the ends and working up, the way you'd comb a child who's tired of being combed. Then rest your hands in your lap for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Patka. A square of cloth tied over a child's topknot, worn before a full turban.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: patka, the square cloth tied over a child's topknot.

carryVoice: Gentle hands: whatever you think about the hair, the comb starts at the ends. That's today.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, on keeping children's hair intact and on the five Ks (kesh, kanga)
